Rational numbers:
A rational number is a number that can be written as a/b, where a and b are integers and b is not 0. All integers, fractions, terminating decimals and repeating decimals are rational. The set of rational numbers is written Q.

A fraction becomes a decimal by dividing the numerator by the denominator. The decimal either stops (like 3/8 = 0.375) or repeats forever (like 1/3 = 0.333...). Every repeating decimal can be turned back into a fraction. For 0.4545..., multiply by 100, subtract the original number, and solve: 99x = 45, so x = 5/11.

Between any two different rational numbers there is another rational number, for example their average. So there are infinitely many rational numbers between any two of them.
Irrational numbers and real numbers:
An irrational number cannot be written as a fraction of two integers. Its decimal form never stops and never repeats. Examples are π, √2 and √3. The square root of a positive integer is irrational unless the integer is a perfect square.

The rational numbers and the irrational numbers together form the real numbers, written R. Every real number matches exactly one point on the number line, and every point on the number line is a real number.

We can place √2 on the number line by drawing the diagonal of a square with side 1. By the Pythagorean theorem its length is √(1^2 + 1^2) = √2. To compare irrational numbers, find the integers they lie between, for example 7 < √50 < 8.
Absolute value:
The absolute value of a number is its distance from 0 on the number line. It is written |x|. Distance is never negative, so |x| is always 0 or positive.

If x ≥ 0, then |x| = x. If x < 0, then |x| = -x. For example, |5| = 5 and |-5| = 5. Also |a| = |-a|, |a·b| = |a|·|b|, and |a - b| is the distance between a and b.

To solve |x| = k with k > 0, there are two answers: x = k or x = -k. If k < 0 there is no solution. When a number inside the bars is an irrational expression, first decide whether it is positive or negative. For example, |√2 - 2| = 2 - √2, because √2 is about 1.41, which is less than 2.
Operations with radicals:
A radical is an expression such as √a. Two rules help with multiplying and dividing: √a · √b = √(ab) and √a / √b = √(a/b), for a ≥ 0 and b > 0. Also √(a^2) = a when a ≥ 0.

To simplify a radical, take out perfect square factors: √72 = √(36 · 2) = 6√2. Radicals can be added or subtracted only when the number under the root is the same: 3√5 + 2√5 = 5√5.

To remove a radical from a denominator, multiply the top and bottom by a suitable number. For 1/√3 multiply by √3/√3 to get √3/3. For 1/(√3 - 1) multiply by (√3 + 1)/(√3 + 1), using (a - b)(a + b) = a^2 - b^2.
Approximation:
An approximation is a number close to the exact value. We use it when the exact value is long or infinite, such as π or √2. To round to a given decimal place, look at the next digit: if it is 5 or more, round up; if it is less than 5, keep the digit.

The error is the difference between the exact value and the approximation: error = |exact - approximate|. The relative error is the error divided by the exact value. It shows how large the error is compared with the number itself.

To approximate a square root, find two numbers whose squares are just below and just above the target, then narrow the interval step by step. For example, 2.6^2 = 6.76 and 2.7^2 = 7.29, so √7 is between 2.6 and 2.7.
